questions.q: What is the Azure Portal primarily used for, per this lesson?
options: Provisioning, configuration, monitoring, cost review, and scaling — resource-level administration, not day-to-day T-SQL work
Writing and tuning complex T-SQL queries as a primary workbench
Replacing SSMS entirely for execution plan analysis
Running SQL Server Agent jobs exclusively
questions.explain: The Portal is described as the resource's control panel, not its workbench — its built-in query editor is thin compared to a real client tool.

questions.q: Why does SSMS remain relevant even for Azure-hosted databases?
options: It has the deepest SQL Server-specific tooling (execution plans, Extended Events, Agent management) and connects to Azure SQL exactly like an on-prem instance
Because Azure Data Studio cannot connect to Azure SQL at all
Because the Azure Portal cannot be used for any administration tasks
Because SSMS is the only tool that supports T-SQL
questions.explain: The T-SQL skills from T-SQL Development run unchanged in SSMS against Azure SQL Database or Managed Instance once connectivity is configured.

questions.q: What is Azure Data Studio's key advantage over SSMS, per this lesson?
options: It's cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux) and supports notebooks and Azure-first extensions, unlike Windows-only SSMS
It has strictly more features than SSMS in every category
It fully replaces the Azure Portal for provisioning tasks
It is the only tool capable of running T-SQL queries
questions.explain: Azure Data Studio isn't a strict SSMS replacement — some deep tooling is still SSMS-only — but it fills the cross-platform and notebook gap SSMS doesn't cover.

questions.q: According to the task-to-tool mapping in this lesson, where would a DBA go to set a cost alert on a database?
options: The Azure Portal
SSMS
Azure Data Studio
None of these tools support cost alerts
questions.explain: Cost alerts, scaling, and firewall rules are Portal-level administration tasks, not query-tool tasks.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say treating any single one of the three tools as sufficient makes the job harder?
options: Because each tool is built for a different kind of task, and a DBA who never opens one (e.g. the Portal) misses capabilities like scaling and cost visibility that no query tool surfaces
Because all three tools are functionally identical and interchangeable
Because only one of the three tools actually works with Azure SQL
Because using multiple tools is against Microsoft's recommended practice
questions.explain: Many DBAs end up running all three, reaching for whichever fits the task in front of them, rather than picking just one.
